Actions on Objectives

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials
Install of TeamPCP Miasma/Hades-compromised npm or PyPI package versions AIDelivery High
Hunts file-system evidence of the specific compromised package@version pairs (ensmallen 0.8.101, mflux-streamlit 0.0.3/0.0.4, embiggen 0.11.97, gpsea 0.9.14, pyphetools 0.9.120, nhmpy 2.4.7, ppkt2synergy 0.1.1) being unpacked into node_modules or site-packages on developer endpoints. Article-specific because it pivots on the named IOCs from the June 3/8 2026 campaign, not on a generic package-install template. Rationale: Uses the exact IOC package names from the kill-chain block (Miasma npm wave June 3 / Hades PyPI wave June 8 2026). Anchoring on node_modules/site-packages path plus the named packages avoids false positives from generic file-create noise. Cross-checked StepSecurity blog and MITRE T1195.002. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally fetching IOC samples for analysis
  • Internal mirror legitimately serving an old, clean version of the package name reused after maintainer recovery
  • Air-gapped reproduction lab unpacking previously archived tarballs
  • CI runner reproducing a historical lockfile resolution for incident-response purposes
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("7z.exe","WinRAR.exe","tar.exe") and FolderPath !contains @"\IR-Samples\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the package@version on disk matches an IOC version; pull package.json/PKG-INFO and the resolved-from URL (npm cache / pip wheel cache). 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, revoke all npm and PyPI tokens accessible from that user (~/.npmrc, ~/.pypirc, keyring), force-rotate any cloud SSO refresh tokens, and block the IOC versions at the internal Artifactory/Nexus mirror. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for other endpoints that resolved the same registry hosts in the last 14 days, audit npm/PyPI publish events under that user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify no downstream repos have lockfiles pinning the bad versions.
let pkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\node_modules\", "/site-packages/")
| where FileName =~ "package.json" or FileName endswith ".dist-info" or FileName =~ "PKG-INFO" or FileName =~ "METADATA"
| where FolderPath has_any (pkgs)
| extend MatchedPkg = tostring(pkgs[array_index_of(pkgs, extract(@"(?i)(?:node_modules[\\/]|site-packages[\\/])([a-z0-9_\-]+)", 1, FolderPath))])
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, MatchedPkg
| order by Timestamp desc
let pkgs = dynamic(["ensmallen","mflux-streamlit","embiggen","gpsea","pyphetools","nhmpy","ppkt2synergy"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\node_modules\", "/site-packages/")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("package.json","PKG-INFO","METADATA") or TargetFilePath endswith ".dist-info"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (pkgs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
title: Miasma/Hades Compromised Package Install

references:

date: 2026/06/16

Package-manager install descendant reads .npmrc / pip.conf credentials AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects credential-bearing config reads (.npmrc, .yarnrc, .yarnrc.yml, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf) by short-lived processes whose ancestor is npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip — the exact harvest behaviour Miasma/Hades use to steal publishing tokens. Article-specific because the file set and parent-process set are taken directly from the campaign write-up. Rationale: Article explicitly names the credential files harvested by Miasma/Hades ("a static token sitting in a .npmrc is not just a hygiene issue, it is the fuel these worms run on"). Pairing the named files with package-manager ancestors gives strong intent signal without flagging routine editor opens. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1552.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/001/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1528
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer running `npm whoami` or `pip config list` which legitimately reads the same config files
  • IDE language-server (VS Code Python/Node extensions) parsing the user's config on workspace open
  • CI bootstrap step that reads .npmrc to set up authenticated proxy
  • Secrets-scanning agent (gitleaks, trufflehog) inventorying dotfiles
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "whoami" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config list" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "config get"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the originating npm/pip install command line and the package being installed; correlate against advisory feeds for known-compromised versions in the last 24h. 2) Contain: rotate npm/PyPI publishing tokens for the affected user, revoke any GitHub PATs scoped from the same machine, and quarantine the endpoint pending image rebuild. 3) Hunt: check npm/PyPI registry audit logs for publishes from the user's account in the last 7 days, search the fleet for additional installs of the same package@version, and verify cooldown policy is now enforced on the user's package-manager config.
let creds = dynamic([".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf"]);
let pmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","node","python","python3"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (creds)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmParents) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmParents)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
let creds = dynamic([".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf"]);
let pmParents = dynamic(["npm.exe","npm-cli.js","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","npm","pip","node","python","python3"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ (creds)
| where ActingProcessName in~ (pmParents) or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any (pmParents)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventType
title: Package Manager Descendant Reads Registry Credentials
id: f5d76a82-3a8d-44e6-b7ef-13c69e2e6451
description: Reads of .npmrc, .yarnrc, bunfig.toml, .pypirc, pip.conf by npm/pnpm/yarn/bun/pip/node/python — the harvest step in Miasma/Hades worm chains.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1552.001
  - attack.credential_access
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith:
      - '\.npmrc'
      - '\.yarnrc'
      - '\.yarnrc.yml'
      - '\bunfig.toml'
      - '\.pypirc'
      - '\pip.conf'
  selection_parent:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\python3.exe'
      - '\pip.exe'
      - '\pip3.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_parent
level: medium
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) (@TargetFilename:(*\\.npmrc OR *\\.yarnrc OR *\\.yarnrc.yml OR *\\bunfig.toml OR *\\.pypirc OR *\\pip.conf) OR @file.path:(*/.npmrc OR */.yarnrc OR */.yarnrc.yml OR */bunfig.toml OR */.pypirc OR */pip.conf)) (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe OR *\\pip.exe OR *\\pip3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */npm OR */pnpm OR */yarn OR */bun OR */python* OR */pip*))
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo
| TargetFileName=/(\\\.npmrc|\\\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\\bunfig\.toml|\\\.pypirc|\\pip\.conf|\/\.npmrc|\/\.yarnrc(\.yml)?|\/bunfig\.toml|\/\.pypirc|\/pip\.conf)$/i
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|python3?|pip3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name IN (".npmrc",".yarnrc",".yarnrc.yml","bunfig.toml",".pypirc","pip.conf")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.action | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | search process_path IN ("*\\node.exe","*\\python.exe","*\\python3","*\\pip*","*\\npm*","*\\yarn*","*\\pnpm*","*\\bun*","*/node","*/python*","*/pip*") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Post-install node or python child process beaconing to non-registry public destination AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for node/python (descended from an npm or pip install) making outbound network connections to public destinations that are NOT the legitimate package registries — the egress channel a Miasma/Hades post-install script would use to exfil harvested tokens or pull the next stage. Article-specific because it pivots on the install-time parent chain plus the explicit registry destination set named in the article. Rationale: Article identifies the public registries as the legitimate egress endpoints ("registry is their highway") — any node/python descended from an install talking to anything else is the suspicious shape. Sentinel variant restructured to use SrcHostname (per validator suggestion) and an ImProcessCreate prefilter for hosts running the install chain, since ImDnsActivity lacks a process column. Cross-checked StepSecurity write-up and MITRE T1071.001. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/prevent-npm-and-python-supply-chain-attacks-on-developer-machines-with-package-configs • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Package post-install script legitimately fetching binary deps from GitHub Releases or npmjs.com (e.g. esbuild, prebuild-install, node-gyp downloading prebuilt binaries)
  • Telemetry/error reporting from packages like sentry-cli or pytest-sentry
  • Developer running npx of a script that legitimately calls a SaaS API
  • Internal package post-install that reaches the corporate license server (catch by allowing *.internal)
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("github.com","githubusercontent.com","objects.githubusercontent.com") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("prebuild-install","node-gyp","esbuild"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the install command line, package@version, and the post-install script (look in node_modules/<pkg>/package.json `scripts.postinstall` or setup.py); reverse the destination domain via WHOIS / passive DNS. 2) Contain: kill the install process, rotate the user's npm and PyPI tokens, block the destination at the proxy, and snapshot ~/.npmrc and ~/.pypirc before image rebuild. 3) Hunt: search the fleet for any other endpoint that DNS-resolved the same destination in the last 14 days, pivot to npm/PyPI publish events under the user's tokens for republished tarballs, and verify the bad package@version is now blocked at the internal mirror.
let pmAncestors = dynamic(["npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","npm","pip"]);
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let installers = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(1d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (pmAncestors) or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ (pmAncestors)
    | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
    | project InstallTime = Timestamp, DeviceId, InstallerPid = ProcessId, InstallerName = FileName, InstallerCmd = ProcessCommandLine;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","node","python","python3")
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any (allowedRegistries))
| join kind=inner installers on $left.DeviceId == $right.DeviceId, $left.InitiatingProcessId == $right.InstallerPid
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, InstallTime, InstallerCmd
| order by Timestamp desc
let allowedRegistries = dynamic(["registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com"]);
let endpointHosts = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("npm","pnpm","yarn","bun","pip","pip3")
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","python","python3")
    | summarize by DvcHostname;
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SrcHostname in (endpointHosts)
| where not (DnsQuery has_any (allowedRegistries))
| where DnsQuery !endswith ".internal" and DnsQuery !endswith ".corp" and DnsQuery !endswith ".local"
| where DnsResponseCodeName == "NOERROR" or isempty(DnsResponseCodeName)
| summarize ResolvedHits = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), Domains = make_set(DnsQuery, 50) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd) @EventID:3 (@Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\python3.exe) OR @process.executable.path:(*/node OR */python OR */python3)) -@DestinationHostname:(*registry.npmjs.org OR *registry.yarnpkg.com OR *pypi.org OR *files.pythonhosted.org OR *npm.pkg.github.com OR *.internal OR *.corp OR *.local)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4) | NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| join({#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName!=/(registry\.npmjs\.org|registry\.yarnpkg\.com|pypi\.org|files\.pythonhosted\.org|npm\.pkg\.github\.com)$/i | ContextImageFileName=/(\\|\/)(node|python3?)(\.exe)?$/i}, field=aid)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node") AND All_Traffic.dest_category="external" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com")) | search NOT (dest="*.internal" OR dest="*.corp") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.app IN ("node.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","python3","node") AND All_Traffic.dest_category="external" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | search NOT (dest IN ("registry.npmjs.org","registry.yarnpkg.com","pypi.org","files.pythonhosted.org","npm.pkg.github.com")) | search NOT (dest="*.internal" OR dest="*.corp") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

SSRF exploitation against self-hosted LobeHub /webapi/proxy (CVE-2026-54157) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POSTs to the unauthenticated /webapi/proxy endpoint on self-hosted LobeHub instances. This is the exact SSRF sink the GHSA reproducer hits — legitimate LobeHub clients in @lobehub/lobehub <=2.1.56 don't POST to this path from the browser, and post-patch every call carries an auth cookie/header. Rationale: Pivots on the exact path string the GHSA names — `/webapi/proxy` — combined with POST method, the only verb the route handler accepts. Path is unique to LobeHub and absent from any other product's URL space, so substring match is high-fidelity. Cross-checked with prior LobeHub /api/proxy advisory (GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc) confirming this is the same code path the original patch missed. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/lobehub/lobe-chat/security/advisories/GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc • https://github.com/lobehub/lobehub/security/advisories/GHSA-3fc8-2r3f-8wrg • https://app.opencve.io/cve/?vendor=lobehub
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal DAST/pen-test scanner (Burp, ZAP, Nuclei) hitting the endpoint during scheduled scans
  • Authenticated LobeHub admin actions against the patched route (post-2.1.56) — auth cookies present
  • Health-check probes from internal monitoring (Uptime Kuma, Pingdom) configured to POST against the path
  • Security researcher PoC traffic from corporate-known IPs
Suppression filter
// add response-side context to drop pen-test scanner noise
| where Status !in ("401","403") // pre-patch route returns 200; suppress auth-rejecting probes against patched instances
| where SrcIP !in (<known scanner CIDR allow list>)
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the request body / Content-Length and Referer for any POST hit to /webapi/proxy. Inspect upstream Set-Cookie reflection in the response — if the response carries a Set-Cookie matching __session/__clerk_db_jwt/__client_uat with Domain=lobehub.com, exploitation is confirmed. 2. Contain: block the source IP at the edge/WAF; deploy emergency WAF rule rejecting POST /webapi/proxy unless Authorization or Clerk session cookie present; upgrade @lobehub/lobehub past 2.1.56 or hot-patch route.ts with checkAuth() wrapper. 3. Hunt: pivot on Vercel egress IP from internal request tracing (Traceparent / X-Vercel-Id leak) to find lateral SSRF use; review Clerk auth logs for sessions established with attacker-injected __session values; check outbound logs for connections from the LobeHub server's egress IP to cloud metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254) or Vercel management plane.
let LobeHubProxyPath = "/webapi/proxy";
union isfuzzy=true
  (W3CIISLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where csMethod =~ "POST" and csUriStem =~ LobeHubProxyPath
     | project TimeGenerated, Source="IIS", SrcIP=cIP, Method=csMethod, Host=sSiteName, URI=csUriStem, UA=csUserAgent, Status=scStatus, Computer),
  (AppServiceHTTPLogs
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where CsMethod =~ "POST" and CsUriStem =~ LobeHubProxyPath
     | project TimeGenerated, Source="AppService", SrcIP=CIp, Method=CsMethod, Host=CsHost, URI=CsUriStem, UA=UserAgent, Status=ScStatus, Computer=CsHost),
  (CommonSecurityLog
     | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
     | where RequestMethod =~ "POST" and RequestURL has LobeHubProxyPath
     | project TimeGenerated, Source=DeviceVendor, SrcIP=SourceIP, Method=RequestMethod, Host=DestinationHostName, URI=RequestURL, UA=RequestClientApplication, Status=tostring(EventOutcome), Computer=DestinationHostName)
| summarize Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(UA, 25), Statuses=make_set(Status, 10) by SrcIP, Host, URI, Source
| order by LastSeen desc

Vulnerable @lobehub/lobehub install (<=2.1.56) detected on managed device AIWeaponization High
Identifies hosts whose Defender TVM inventory lists @lobehub/lobehub at 2.1.56 or earlier — the version range where /webapi/proxy is missing the checkAuth() middleware. Pairs with the exploitation hunt to convert exposure into patching priority and to flag internet-facing devices first. Rationale: Hooks the exact CVE ID assigned in the advisory (CVE-2026-54157) and the package name @lobehub/lobehub at the inventory layer. Internet-facing devices first because the SSRF is unauthenticated — any LobeHub instance exposed to the public internet on <=2.1.56 is directly exploitable. No second source needed beyond the GHSA itself; vendor advisory IS the corroboration for the version range. Cross-checked against: • https://www.npmjs.com/package/@lobehub/lobehub • https://github.com/lobehub/lobehub/security/advisories/GHSA-3fc8-2r3f-8wrg

Corporate browser POST to app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy with text/plain CSRF form shape AIDelivery Medium
Detects the exact request shape from the GHSA's CSRF PoC: a browser POSTing to app.lobehub.com/webapi/proxy with Content-Type text/plain;charset=UTF-8 and a Referer that isn't lobehub.com. Legitimate users navigate to LobeHub via /chat, not by POSTing JSON-less form data to the proxy route — this shape only appears when a user has landed on an attacker page that auto-submits the cookie-injection form. Rationale: Pivots on three article-specific signals: the exact host `app.lobehub.com`, the exact path `/webapi/proxy`, and the cross-origin Referer mismatch that the GHSA's `<form enctype="text/plain">` PoC produces. The text/plain content-type is itself a CSRF telltale because it's the only enctype that bypasses CORS preflight while letting the attacker control the request body. Falcon path uses DNS-only correlation because FDR's NetworkConnectIP4 doesn't carry URI paths. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xmwj-c75x-6346 • https://github.com/lobehub/lobe-chat/security/advisories/GHSA-mxhq-xw3g-rphc
ATT&CKT1190 T1539
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Engineer testing the SSRF locally with curl against the production endpoint
  • Browser extensions that prefetch lobehub.com endpoints
  • Empty Referer due to strict Referrer-Policy on legitimate LobeHub navigation
  • Internal red-team CSRF exercise traffic
  • Bookmark click landing directly on /chat that pivots through /webapi/proxy in newer client versions
Suppression filter
// drop the most common benign case: empty referer on direct-navigation or strict-referrer policy
| where isnotempty(Referer)
// suppress known internal pentest egress
| where SrcIpAddr !in (<pentest CIDR>)
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full request — Referer header points to the attacker-hosted CSRF page (often a freshly-registered domain or a paste/gist). Capture the URL in the POST body (the field name in text/plain form encoding IS the URL the SSRF will fetch). Resolve that URL — if it returns Set-Cookie with Domain=lobehub.com, confirmed CSRF in flight. 2. Contain: block the attacker domain at proxy/DNS; force-logout the affected user from lobehub.com (sessions issued post-event may be attacker-fixed); rotate Clerk session cookies for the user; alert user not to log into LobeHub until cookies are cleared. 3. Hunt: pivot to all corporate users who hit the same attacker Referer in the past 30d; check email/IM logs for the attacker URL distribution vector; query Clerk audit (if available) for session establishment with __session values matching the injected pattern.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "app.lobehub.com" and RemoteUrl has "/webapi/proxy"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe","opera.exe","iexplore.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          BrowserBinary=InitiatingProcessFileName,
          BrowserParent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName
    | project DeviceId, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, BrowserCmd=ProcessCommandLine
  ) on DeviceName, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where HttpHostName =~ "app.lobehub.com" and Url has "/webapi/proxy"
| where HttpRequestHeaderReferer !has "lobehub.com"
     or HttpResponseHeaderContentType has "text/plain"
     or isempty(HttpRequestHeaderReferer)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, SrcHostname,
          Url, HttpHostName, HttpMethod,
          Referer=HttpRequestHeaderReferer,
          ContentType=HttpResponseHeaderContentType,
          UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent,
          DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI /screenshot or /pdf path traversal via output_path parameter AIExploitation Medium
Hunts HTTP POSTs to the Crawl4AI Docker API endpoints `/screenshot` and `/pdf` carrying an `output_path` JSON body parameter with `..` traversal sequences or absolute paths outside `/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs/`. Targets pre-patch exploitation of CWE-22 file-write giving an attacker overwrite primitives on any appuser-writable location. Rationale: Combines URL/query inspection for `..`/`%2e%2e` against the article's named endpoints (`/screenshot`, `/pdf`) and the `output_path` parameter mentioned in the fix description (`validate_output_path()`). Defender KQL pivots to the file-write effect outside the patched-default `CRAWL4AI_OUTPUT_DIR=/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs` — the only signal available when body capture isn't shipped.
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Crawl4AI users supplying output filenames containing `..` in the page title that ends up in URL-rewritten artifact paths
  • Penetration testers and security scanners (Burp/ZAP) probing the endpoint
  • Crawl4AI internal temp-file moves by playwright writing browser cache outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs
  • Admin operator manually invoking the API for export to a shared volume mount
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "--user-data-dir" and FolderPath has "playwright")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm Crawl4AI version (<=0.8.6 is vulnerable), pull the full request URL and source IP, check whether Authorization header was present and which token authenticated. 2) Contain: block source IP at edge, rotate any secrets reachable from /etc on the container (especially if AWS/GCP creds were sitting in appuser-writable paths), force-upgrade Crawl4AI to the patched release, set CRAWL4AI_OUTPUT_DIR explicitly. 3) Hunt: pivot on source IP across the SSRF UC (cloud-metadata egress) and any /execute_js calls in the same session — same actor likely chained vulnerabilities; review file writes outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs in the last 14 days from the same container.
// Detect the *effect* of the Crawl4AI path-traversal: chromium/playwright/python writing to paths outside /tmp/crawl4ai-outputs/ on the Crawl4AI container host
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome","chromium","headless_shell","python","python3","uvicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","uvicorn","fastapi","playwright")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where not(FolderPath startswith "/tmp/crawl4ai-outputs/")
| where FolderPath startswith "/etc/" or FolderPath startswith "/root/" or FolderPath startswith "/home/" or FolderPath startswith "/var/" or FolderPath startswith "/usr/" or FileName in~ ("authorized_keys",".bashrc",".profile",".bash_profile","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// HTTP POSTs to /screenshot or /pdf with traversal markers in URL/query — body inspection requires WAF/proxy that captures it
let Lookback = 7d;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where Url has_any ("/screenshot","/pdf")
| where Url has ".." or Url has "%2e%2e" or UrlOriginal has ".." or UrlOriginal has "%2e%2e"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, UrlOriginal, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI container SSRF egress to cloud metadata or RFC1918 ranges AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the Crawl4AI Docker container's browser or python process reaching the AWS/GCP/Azure metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) or any RFC 1918 / loopback / link-local address — the exploitable signal for the /crawl, /md, /llm, /screenshot, /pdf, webhook and /execute_js SSRF chains. Also covers the IPv6-mapped IPv4 bypass form by detecting on the resolved IP rather than the URL string. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 169.254.169.254 as the SSRF target and calls out RFC 1918, loopback, link-local as the blocklist scope. Detecting at the network layer also catches the IPv6-mapped IPv4 bypass (`[::ffff:169.254.169.254]`) noted in vuln #7, because the actual outbound socket resolves to the real IPv4 destination regardless of URL encoding. Pivoting on chromium/python parent process scopes to the Crawl4AI worker rather than legitimate metadata pollers like cloud-agent daemons.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.005 T1046
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Crawl4AI legitimately crawling an internal documentation site on RFC1918
  • SSDP / mDNS chatter to 169.254.255.255 broadcast (not 169.254.169.254 but adjacent range)
  • Health checks from container orchestrator hitting localhost on a non-standard port
  • Cloud agents like aws-ssm-agent / google-osconfig-agent legitimately polling metadata — exclude if also instrumented
  • Operator-driven test crawl against staging environments in the same VPC
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP startswith "127." and RemotePort in (5000, 8000, 8080, 11235))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which HTTP endpoint triggered the egress by joining to web-access logs in the same time window (look for POST/GET to /crawl, /crawl/stream, /md, /llm, /crawl/job, /llm/job, /screenshot, /pdf, /execute_js) and capture the URL parameter that was crawled. 2) Contain: rotate any IAM role / service-account credentials reachable from the metadata endpoint on that host (the SSRF likely exfiltrated them), block the source IP that submitted the crawl request, upgrade Crawl4AI to patched version. 3) Hunt: check CloudTrail/Azure Activity for the rotated principal's recent activity (look for unfamiliar IPs, S3 enumeration, IAM enumeration); scan all Crawl4AI deployment images for version <=0.8.6; correlate to UC1 (path traversal) and UC4 (/execute_js) hits from the same source IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome","chromium","headless_shell","python","python3","uvicorn")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","uvicorn server:app","playwright")

Unauthenticated access to Crawl4AI /monitor/* endpoints incl. destructive cleanup AIExploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to Crawl4AI monitor router paths (/monitor/, /monitor/ws, /monitor/actions/cleanup) where the Authorization header is missing — the pre-patch state allowed any caller to invoke destructive endpoints without `token_dep`. Targets CWE-306 exposure including the destructive `/monitor/actions/cleanup` route. Rationale: Endpoint paths come straight from the fix description (`dependencies=[Depends(token_dep)]` added to monitor router; `/monitor/ws` WebSocket explicitly noted; `/monitor/actions/cleanup` called out as destructive). A 200/101/204 response with no Authorization header on /monitor/actions/* on a vulnerable build is unambiguous post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal ops dashboard polling /monitor/health from a trusted IP without auth (depends on deployment posture)
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probe to /monitor
  • Prometheus/Grafana scrapers hitting /monitor/metrics from inside the mesh
  • Operator manually visiting /monitor/ws via browser dev session during upgrade
  • Load-balancer health checks misconfigured to GET /monitor
Suppression filter
| where not (SrcIpAddr in ("10.0.0.10","10.0.0.11") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("kube-probe","GoogleHC","ELB-HealthChecker"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which monitor sub-path was hit, look for 200/101 responses, count requests by source IP over the prior 24h, check Crawl4AI version. 2) Contain: block source IP at edge, rotate CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN, upgrade to patched version, restart container so WebSocket connections from the unauth period are dropped, verify no /monitor/actions/cleanup was successfully invoked (this would wipe job state). 3) Hunt: pivot on source IP for UC1 (path-traversal) and UC2 (SSRF) — actors enumerating /monitor often probe the file-write and SSRF surfaces in the same session; check whether any forged JWTs signed with the default `mysecret` granted privileged operations elsewhere.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/monitor","/monitor/ws","/monitor/actions/cleanup","/monitor/actions")
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","101","204")
| extend IsDestructive = iff(Url has "/monitor/actions/", true, false)
| extend AuthMissing = iff(isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) or HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization == "", true, false)
| where IsDestructive == true or AuthMissing == true
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, IsDestructive, AuthMissing
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI /execute_js endpoint invocation (pre-patch arbitrary JS / SSRF) AIExploitation Medium
Detects HTTP POSTs to the Crawl4AI `/execute_js` endpoint, which pre-patch ran arbitrary user-supplied JavaScript inside the server's headless browser launched with `--disable-web-security`. Post-patch this endpoint is opt-in via `CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED`, so any hit on a fleet that didn't explicitly enable it is suspicious. Also flags IPv6-mapped IPv4 SSRF bypass patterns (`[::ffff:169.254.169.254]`) appearing in URL bodies on any crawl endpoint. Rationale: `/execute_js` is named verbatim in vuln #5 and the patch makes it opt-in via `CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED`, so any hit on a fleet that didn't explicitly enable it is high-fidelity. The IPv6-mapped IPv4 patterns (`::ffff:` literal and URL-encoded `%3A%3Affff%3A`) come verbatim from vuln #7's bypass example and are otherwise virtually never seen in benign URL params. Combining the two on the same alert reduces rule count without losing signal — both are crawl/JS API abuse.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007 T1552.005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate operator with `CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=true` running smoke tests against /execute_js
  • Pentesters / Red team exercising the patched endpoint to confirm hardening
  • Crawl4AI integration test suite that exercises /execute_js as part of CI
  • Researchers crawling URLs whose page content legitimately contains `::ffff:` text in query strings
  • Internal docs site whose URL fragment happens to include `169.254.169.254` as content
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether `CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED` is set on the workload — if false, any /execute_js POST is attack traffic. Capture the JS body submitted (from WAF body-capture or app log), source IP, and any 200 response. 2) Contain: set `CRAWL4AI_EXECUTE_JS_ENABLED=false` (default post-patch), upgrade to patched Crawl4AI, block source IP, rotate any credentials the embedded JS could have reached via XHR with `--disable-web-security` enabled. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2 — the same session almost certainly attempted metadata-IP exfil via the JS payload's `fetch()` to 169.254.169.254; also look for any FileWritten by chromium under unusual paths (XHR + path traversal chain) and check the same source IP for /monitor/* probes in UC3.
let CrawlEndpoints = dynamic(["/crawl","/crawl/stream","/md","/llm","/crawl/job","/llm/job","/screenshot","/pdf"]);

| extend IsSsrfBypassPayload = (Url has "::ffff:" or Url has "%3A%3Affff%3A" or Url has "169.254.169.254" or Url has "metadata.google.internal" or UrlOriginal has "::ffff:" or UrlOriginal has "169.254.169.254")
| extend HitsCrawlEndpoint = Url has_any (CrawlEndpoints)
| where IsExecuteJs == true or (HitsCrawlEndpoint == true and IsSsrfBypassPayload == true)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, UrlOriginal, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, IsExecuteJs, IsSsrfBypassPayload
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI CVE-2026-53753 AST Sandbox-Escape Payload in POST /crawl AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP POST requests to a Crawl4AI /crawl endpoint whose body or query carries Python frame-walk primitives (gi_frame, f_back, f_builtins) or a JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema containing __import__. This is the pre-auth RCE attempt against a Crawl4AI Docker container (<=0.8.6). Rationale: Targets the four exploit primitives explicitly named in the advisory body (gi_frame, f_back, f_builtins, __import__) combined with the article-specified ingress: POST /crawl carrying a JsonCssExtractionStrategy schema. These strings effectively never appear in legitimate /crawl traffic, giving near-zero FP. Defender XDR has no HTTP-body-bearing table so defender_kql/falcon are empty — body inspection lives at WAF/reverse-proxy. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qxjp-w3pj-48m7 • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006 T1480.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Tenable/Qualys) replaying the CVE-2026-53753 PoC against staging
  • Red-team / pentest exercises validating Crawl4AI exposure
  • Security researchers testing their own Crawl4AI deployment after upgrade
  • Bug-bounty traffic to public Crawl4AI gateways (rare, but noisy when it happens)
Suppression filter
and SourceIP !in ("<authorized-scanner-cidr>")
   and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei", "qualys", "tenable", "Nessus")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): identify the source IP, geolocation, and whether the Crawl4AI host responded 2xx vs 4xx/5xx — a 2xx with a body length >0 means the sandbox escape likely executed. Pull the full request body and any subsequent egress from the Crawl4AI container. Step 2 (contain): block the source IP at WAF, isolate the Crawl4AI container/host, and enable CRAWL4AI_API_TOKEN JWT auth as an interim workaround if upgrading isn't immediate. Rotate any secrets exposed inside the container (env vars, mounted credentials, cloud metadata creds). Step 3 (hunt): pivot on the host — query UC2 (post-exploit shell spawn) for the same DeviceId/host within ±10 min of the request; check outbound DNS/IP from the container for second-stage download or exfil; inventory all Crawl4AI deployments via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for SoftwareName 'crawl4ai' Version <= 0.8.6.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/crawl"
| where Message has_any ("gi_frame", "f_back", "f_builtins", "JsonCssExtractionStrategy", "__import__")
   or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("gi_frame", "f_back", "f_builtins")
   or DeviceCustomString2 has_any ("gi_frame", "f_back", "f_builtins")
   or DeviceCustomString3 has_any ("gi_frame", "f_back", "f_builtins")
   or RequestContext has_any ("gi_frame", "f_back", "f_builtins")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, DestinationIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message, DeviceCustomString1, DeviceCustomString2
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crawl4AI Server (uvicorn/python) Spawning Shell or Recon Tool (Post-Exploit CVE-2026-53753) AIInstallation High
Hunts the post-exploitation shape of CVE-2026-53753: the Crawl4AI Python server process (typically uvicorn/gunicorn/python invoking server:app or crawl4ai) spawning a shell, curl/wget, or reading credential/env files. Crawl4AI by design does not shell out — any /bin/sh child of the server is high-fidelity post-RCE evidence. Rationale: Article states the exploit results in 'arbitrary code execution inside the Docker container' via `__import__('os')` — meaning the Crawl4AI server (uvicorn/gunicorn/python running crawl4ai.server or server:app) is the parent of any shelled-out child. Crawl4AI's legitimate workload is HTTP fetching, not shell invocation, so any /bin/sh child of the server is extremely high signal. Recon strings (/etc/passwd, /proc/self/environ, 169.254.169.254 cloud-metadata) target the article-stated impact: 'read/write files, and exfiltrate secrets'. The dev-tool negative filter drops jupyter/pytest/pip noise that lives in the same parent space. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qxjp-w3pj-48m7 • https://github.com/unclecode/crawl4ai/security
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Python data-science containers using subprocess to invoke shell utilities (Jupyter/pytest workflows — covered by filter)
  • Container entrypoint shell scripts started by a python launcher
  • Crawl4AI sidecar healthcheck/diagnostic scripts (rare; if they exist, allowlist the specific cmdline)
  • pip install <package> running post-install shell hooks during image builds
  • Legitimate admin debugging via docker exec into the crawl4ai container (parent will not be uvicorn though — usually init/runc)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel","pip install","setup.py","pytest","conda","poetry run"))
  and not(ProcessCommandLine startswith "/bin/sh -c /opt/crawl4ai/healthcheck.sh")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): pull the exact ProcessCommandLine and confirm the parent is the running Crawl4AI server (uvicorn server:app); correlate with UC1 hits on the same host within the prior 10 minutes to find the originating /crawl request and source IP. Step 2 (contain): isolate the container (docker pause / kubectl cordon), snapshot for forensics, then rotate every secret reachable from the container — mounted Kubernetes service-account tokens, cloud IMDS-issued creds (169.254.169.254), env vars, and any API keys in CRAWL4AI_* env. Step 3 (hunt): expand to all hosts running crawl4ai <= 0.8.6 via DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory; check egress from the container for second-stage download (curl/wget to unfamiliar IPs) and for outbound to cloud-metadata IPs; review WAF for /crawl POSTs in the prior 24h carrying the UC1 sandbox-escape strings.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","uvicorn server:app","crawl4ai.server")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","printenv","/proc/self/environ","169.254.169.254","metadata.google.internal")
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel","pip install","setup.py","pytest"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildImage = FolderPath,
          ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python","python3","uvicorn","gunicorn")
   or ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("crawl4ai","uvicorn server:app","crawl4ai.server")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","ash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat")
   or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/etc/passwd","/etc/shadow","printenv","/proc/self/environ","169.254.169.254","metadata.google.internal")
| where not(ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("jupyter","ipykernel","pip install","setup.py","pytest"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT

| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:

            - '\wscript.exe'

            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive hash match
level: critical

Multiple JetBrains IDE plugins caught stealing AI keys

Aikido
2026-06-16 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A coordinated campaign of at least 15 JetBrains IDE plugins, published under seven vendor accounts, exfiltrates the AI provider API key you paste into their settings. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

ATT&CKT1176 T1190 T1195.002
IPs39.107.60.51
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugin ID present in IDE plugins folder · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE process connects to malicious plugin C2 39.107.60.51 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Inspected HTTP POST to /api/software/ with attacker's static X-Api-Key header · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE process connects to malicious plugin C2 39.107.60.51 AICommand & Control Medium
JetBrains IDEs run plugins inside the IDE's JVM, so a direct outbound connection from idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / java.exe to the hardcoded attacker IP 39.107.60.51 is a high-fidelity indicator that one of the 15 malicious AI-assistant plugins has just exfiltrated a stored AI provider API key. The IP is single-purpose and sits in Alibaba Cloud (AS37963) with no legitimate use case for a developer endpoint. Rationale: 39.107.60.51 is the hardcoded plaintext-HTTP exfil server named verbatim in the Aikido write-up (Block 3 / IoC list). A single hit from a developer endpoint is sufficient — no other legitimate caller has been observed for this address.
ATT&CKT1041 T1567.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher manually probing the C2 from a sandboxed dev VM
  • Outbound proxy / firewall liveness check explicitly configured to ping the published IOC
  • Sinkhole / decoy traffic from a deliberate honeypot deployment
  • Defender / EDR re-detonation of an archived malicious plugin during retro-hunt
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory / file-event history for the affected host and list every plugin under %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins — flag any whose XML plugin id matches the 15 IoCs (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.). Capture the InitiatingProcessAccountUpn — that user typed at least one AI provider API key into the plugin settings. 2) Contain: immediately revoke and rotate any OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow API keys belonging to the user; uninstall the offending plugin and remove its directory; block 39.107.60.51 at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot on plugin id across all developer endpoints (DeviceFileEvents FolderPath has 'JetBrains' and 'plugins'); check OpenAI / DeepSeek billing portals for unusual usage in the last 60 days from unfamiliar IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "39.107.60.51"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, Url, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Outbound Connection to JetBrains Marketplace Plugin AI-Key Stealer C2
id: 7c5e1c34-9a4b-4f2e-9b1a-2d6c0e7b1c01
description: Detects outbound network connection to 39.107.60.51, the hardcoded C2 used by 15 malicious JetBrains plugins (Aikido 2026-06-16) to exfiltrate user-supplied OpenAI/DeepSeek/SiliconFlow API keys.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/multiple-jetbrains-ide-plugins-caught-stealing-ai-keys
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.exfiltration
logsource:
  category: network_connection
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp: '39.107.60.51'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:39.107.60.51
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4=39.107.60.51
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="39.107.60.51" by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port, All_Traffic.app, All_Traffic.transport | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Inspected HTTP POST to /api/software/ with attacker's static X-Api-Key header AIActions on Objectives Medium
Where a TLS-inspecting proxy or web gateway records full request URLs and headers, this catches the actual exfil call — POST http://39.107.60.51/api/software/<name> carrying the hardcoded static token X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D and a JSON body containing the victim's apiKey field. This is the most precise rule possible against the campaign because both the URL path and the token are unique to the malicious plugin codebase. Rationale: Both the URI path /api/software/ AND the destination 39.107.60.51 are taken verbatim from the deobfuscated save() handler in the article (Block 2). Either signal alone is unique to this campaign; together they leave no plausible false positive.
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal pentester replaying the published IOC against a sanctioned target
  • Threat-intel platform retrospectively decoding archived sandbox PCAPs
  • Vendor security scanner generating synthetic exfil traffic for control validation
  • Honeypot infrastructure deliberately calling the IOC
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract SourceIP / InitiatingProcessAccountUpn from the POST — that user's stored AI keys are already at the attacker. Identify which JetBrains IDE process (idea64.exe / pycharm64.exe / java.exe) made the call so the responsible plugin id can be tied back via plugin XML. 2) Contain: revoke and rotate every AI provider key (OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow) associated with that developer; uninstall the offending plugin directory and clear the plugin's settings file; block 39.107.60.51 and any URI containing /api/software/ at the egress proxy. 3) Hunt: search 90 days of proxy logs for any prior POST to the same URI; pivot on the static header value 'F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D' in raw proxy capture if header logging is enabled; query AI provider billing dashboards for spend anomalies on the victim's keys.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51" or RemoteUrl has "/api/software/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "39.107.60.51" or RequestURL has "/api/software/"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Malicious JetBrains Plugin Exfil POST to /api/software/ on 39.107.60.51
id: 9e4a37b2-1f0b-4e1d-9a52-bb3a78db17c2
description: HTTP POST to attacker server 39.107.60.51 with URI containing /api/software/ — the verbatim exfil endpoint used by 15 malicious JetBrains Marketplace plugins (Aikido 2026-06-16) to steal OpenAI / DeepSeek / SiliconFlow API keys.
references:
  - https://www.aikido.dev/blog/multiple-jetbrains-ide-plugins-caught-stealing-ai-keys
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:

  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.exfiltration
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
