SprySOCKS WIN_DRV component .dat filenames written to disk (RawWNPF / DriverLoader) AIInstallation High
Hunts file-write events for the hard-coded SprySOCKS WIN_DRV driver-component filenames disclosed by ESET — KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat (RawWNPF rootkit driver) and KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat (encrypted DriverLoader). Any match is a high-confidence indicator of WIN_DRV deployment. Rationale: Filenames are hard-coded SprySOCKS WIN_DRV components disclosed in ESET's report. No legitimate software ships files matching the K[WX]1B5206BDC1743**.dat pattern; the regex anchors catch sibling variants under the same naming convention. Any hit is investigate-immediately. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1014/
ATT&CKT1014 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-research sandbox detonation environments storing malware samples with original filenames preserved
  • Forensic image acquisition tooling unpacking IR evidence on a managed endpoint
  • Security analyst downloading the ESET IOC bundle to their workstation
  • Honeypot or deception VMs intentionally seeded with these filenames for canary alerting
Suppression filter
and not FolderPath has_any ("\\sandbox\\", "\\malware-samples\\", "\\ir-evidence\\", "\\quarantine\\")
Response runbook
Triage: capture SHA256 of the dropped file and the InitiatingProcess that wrote it; cross-check against VirusTotal and ESET — a confirmed hash match is a critical incident requiring no further triage. Contain: isolate the host, kill the writing process tree, quarantine the file, and capture memory before reboot to preserve the kernel-driver state for forensics. Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 of the loader across the org, look for the scheduled task that triggered the DLL side-loading chain in the prior 24h, hunt for the kernel-driver service registration (UC2) and the spoolsv→svchost chain (UC1), and review egress for TCP/UDP/WebSocket callbacks from svchost/spoolsv lineage.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileRenamed", "FileModified")
| where FileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
   or FileName matches regex @"^K[WX]1B5206BDC1743[A-Z0-9]{2}\.dat$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("KW1B5206BDC1743FP.dat", "KX1B5206BDC1743DD.dat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Inbound exploit POST to FortiSandbox tracer-behavior endpoint (CVE-2026-39808) · [LLM] Unauthenticated JRPC API access to FortiSandbox (CVE-2026-39813)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Path traversal patterns in URIs to FortiSandbox (CVE-2025-61624 chain)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Anomalous outbound C2 from FortiSandbox appliance to non-Fortinet infrastructure
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Inbound exploit POST to FortiSandbox tracer-behavior endpoint (CVE-2026-39808) AIDelivery High
Detects HTTP requests targeting the FortiSandbox /fortisandbox/job-detail/tracer-behavior endpoint, where CVE-2026-39808 unauthenticated OS command injection is exploited. Flags POSTs containing shell metacharacters or unusual payload sizes that match the public PoC pattern observed by Defused in active exploitation. Rationale: Endpoint string /fortisandbox/job-detail/tracer-behavior is the confirmed CVE-2026-39808 sink per helpnetsecurity.com and cryptika.com PoC writeups. POST + shell metacharacters in URL/body is the exploit's canonical shape. Cross-checked: Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-100, helpnetsecurity, runzero asset post. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/16/fortinet-fortisandbox-vulnerabilities-cve-2026-39813-cve-2026-39808/ • https://www.cryptika.com/poc-exploit-released-for-fortisandbox-vulnerability-that-allows-attacker-to-execute-commands/ • https://www.runzero.com/blog/fortinet-fortisandbox/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tenable/Qualys/Nessus authenticated vulnerability scans probing the CVE-2026-39808 plugin check
  • Fortinet TAC support engineers validating the patch on customer appliances
  • Internal red-team / purple-team exercises rehearsing the public PoC
  • Pre-prod / staging FortiSandbox upgrade verification scripts that POST sample jobs
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (dynamic(["10.10.20.5", "10.10.20.6"]))  // exclude authorized scanner subnets
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus", "Qualys", "Tenable", "FortinetTAC")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm source IP — is it an authorized scanner (cross-reference with Tenable/Qualys schedule), Fortinet support session (check ticket queue), or unknown external? Pull the full POST body from WAF/proxy logs and inspect for unescaped `;`, `|`, backtick, or `$(...)` constructs. 2) Contain: if source is external/unknown and shell metacharacters are present, block the source IP at the perimeter and isolate the FortiSandbox management interface from the internet pending patch verification (confirm appliance is on 4.4.9+ or 5.0.6+). 3) Hunt: pivot to outbound connections from the FortiSandbox IP for the next 24h (UC4), check FortiSandbox audit logs for new admin accounts, modified detection profiles, or disabled scanning modules, and review sandbox verdicts for the past week for unexpected 'clean' results.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/fortisandbox/job-detail/tracer-behavior"
   or AdditionalFields has "/fortisandbox/job-detail/tracer-behavior"
| extend ShellMeta = extract(@"(?i)(%3[Bb]|%26|%7[Cc]|%60|%24%28|;|\||&|`|\$\()", 0, RemoteUrl)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ShellMeta
| order by Timestamp desc
let FortiSandboxHosts = dynamic(["fortisandbox", "fsa", "FSA"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet" or DestinationHostName has_any (FortiSandboxHosts)
| where RequestURL has "/fortisandbox/job-detail/tracer-behavior"
| extend ShellMeta = extract(@"(?i)(%3[Bb]|%26|%7[Cc]|%60|%24%28|;|\||&|`|\$\()", 0, RequestURL)
| extend BodyShellMeta = extract(@"(?i)(%3[Bb]|%26|%7[Cc]|%60|;|\||`|\$\()", 0, tostring(RequestContext))
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or isnotempty(ShellMeta) or isnotempty(BodyShellMeta)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod,
          RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ShellMeta, BodyShellMeta, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated JRPC API access to FortiSandbox (CVE-2026-39813) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for HTTP requests to the FortiSandbox JRPC (JSON-RPC) API where CVE-2026-39813 auth bypass is exploited via specially crafted requests. Flags requests to /jrpc paths that succeed without prior authentication, particularly from external or non-FortiGate sources on FortiSandbox 4.4.0-4.4.8 / 5.0.0-5.0.5. Rationale: Help Net Security and Fortinet PSIRT FG-IR-26-112 identify the FortiSandbox JRPC API as the auth-bypass vector for CVE-2026-39813. Hunting on JRPC URI patterns from non-FortiGate sources catches both PoC validation and live exploitation. Cross-checked: helpnetsecurity, securityweek.com. Cross-checked against: • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/04/16/fortinet-fortisandbox-vulnerabilities-cve-2026-39813-cve-2026-39808/ • https://www.securityweek.com/fortinet-patches-critical-fortisandbox-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FortiGate appliances submitting samples to FortiSandbox via JRPC (whitelist FortiGate management IPs)
  • FortiAnalyzer / FortiManager API integration polling sandbox verdicts
  • SIEM/SOAR enrichment workflows hitting the FortiSandbox API for IOC lookups
  • Customer-built integration scripts using documented JRPC API
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (FortiGateMgmtIPs)
| where SourceIP !in (FortiAnalyzerIPs)
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("FortiGate", "FortiAnalyzer", "FortiManager")
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify the SourceIP against the inventory of FortiGate / FortiAnalyzer / SOAR integrations authorized to call the FortiSandbox JRPC API. External or unrecognized internal source → escalate. Inspect the JRPC request body for unauthenticated calls (no session cookie / API token) that nonetheless return HTTP 200. 2) Contain: if external/unknown, block SourceIP at perimeter, force a session reset on the FortiSandbox web UI, and rotate any local admin credentials on the appliance. Confirm appliance is patched to 4.4.9 / 5.0.6+. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (tracer-behavior POSTs) from the same SourceIP, review FortiSandbox audit log for any privileged operations (config change, admin add, scan-engine modification) in the 60 minutes following the JRPC hit.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/jrpc", "/api/jrpc", "/jsonrpc")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("fortisandbox", "fsa")
   or AdditionalFields has_any ("fortisandbox", "fsa")
| summarize RequestCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp),
            URLs = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| where RequestCount > 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
let FortiSandboxAssets = dynamic(["fortisandbox", "fsa-", "FSA-"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor =~ "Fortinet"
| where DestinationHostName has_any (FortiSandboxAssets)
     or DestinationServiceName has_any (FortiSandboxAssets)
| where RequestURL has_any ("/jrpc", "/api/jrpc", "/jsonrpc")
| extend IsExternal = iff(SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "172.16." and SourceIP !startswith "172.17." and SourceIP !startswith "172.18." and SourceIP !startswith "172.19." and SourceIP !startswith "172.2" and SourceIP !startswith "172.30." and SourceIP !startswith "172.31." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168.", true, false)
| summarize RequestCount = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            URIs = make_set(RequestURL, 10),
            Methods = make_set(RequestMethod),
            UAs = make_set(RequestClientApplication, 5),
            Statuses = make_set(EventOutcome)
            by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, IsExternal
| where IsExternal == true or RequestCount > 5
| order by FirstSeen desc

Path traversal patterns in URIs to FortiSandbox (CVE-2025-61624 chain) AIExploitation Medium
Detects URI patterns containing directory traversal sequences targeting FortiSandbox appliances. CVE-2025-61624 requires high privileges but Defused notes it was 'very likely chained with another security issue' — early detection of the traversal stage flags exploit chains before privilege escalation completes. Rationale: Article explicitly states CVE-2025-61624 path traversal was 'very likely chained with another security issue' due to its high-privilege prerequisite — making the traversal pattern itself the earliest detectable artifact of a chain attempt. Encoded variants (%2e%2e%2f, %2f, %5c) cover common WAF-evasion encodings. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-fortinet-fortisandbox-flaws-now-exploited-in-attacks/
ATT&CKT1083 T1068 T1574
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized DAST scanners (Burp Suite Pro, OWASP ZAP, Nessus web plugin set) probing for path traversal in scheduled scans
  • Legitimate FortiSandbox file submission UI that may include `..` literally in user-supplied filenames passed through URL parameters
  • Compliance tooling (PCI scans) exercising traversal payloads as part of baseline testing
  • Internal red-team exercises documented in change-control
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (AuthorizedScannerIPs)
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp", "OWASP ZAP", "Nessus", "Qualys", "Nuclei")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull full URI, decode all percent-encoded sequences, and identify the traversal target (does it walk toward /etc/, /sandbox/conf/, /var/log/, or admin config paths?). Check SourceIP against authorized scanner inventory. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, block SourceIP and trigger session invalidation on the appliance; review whether the request returned HTTP 200 (successful traversal) vs 4xx. 3) Hunt: pivot to authenticated API requests from the same SourceIP in the prior 30 minutes (CVE-2025-61624 needs high privs — look for a paired auth-bypass like UC2), and check FortiSandbox audit log for file reads outside the expected web-root.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl matches regex @"(?i)(\.\./|\.\.%2[fF]|%2[eE]%2[eE]%2[fF]|%2[eE]%2[eE]/|\.\.%5[cC])"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("fortisandbox", "fsa-", "job-detail", "/api/")
   or AdditionalFields has_any ("fortisandbox", "fsa-")
| extend TraversalDepth = countof(RemoteUrl, "..")
| where TraversalDepth >= 2
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, TraversalDepth
| order by Timestamp desc
let FortiSandboxAssets = dynamic(["fortisandbox", "fsa-", "FSA-"]);
let TraversalRegex = @"(?i)(\.\./|\.\.%2[fF]|%2[eE]%2[eE]%2[fF]|%2[eE]%2[eE]/|\.\.%5[cC])";
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationHostName has_any (FortiSandboxAssets)
     or DestinationServiceName has_any (FortiSandboxAssets)
| where RequestURL matches regex TraversalRegex
| extend TraversalDepth = countof(RequestURL, "..")
| where TraversalDepth >= 2
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod,
          RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, TraversalDepth, EventOutcome
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Path Traversal Patterns Targeting FortiSandbox (CVE-2025-61624)
id: a7c4e082-9f15-4b3d-8e6a-1c5b2d4f7e93
status: experimental
description: Detects URI patterns containing directory traversal sequences (.../, ..%2f, %2e%2e%2f, etc.) targeting FortiSandbox appliances. CVE-2025-61624 is the authenticated path-traversal flaw Defused noted as likely chained with another security issue.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16

WEB

Anomalous outbound C2 from FortiSandbox appliance to non-Fortinet infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Detects post-exploit C2 callback or data exfiltration originating from a compromised FortiSandbox appliance. After successful RCE via CVE-2026-39808/39813/26083, attackers commonly use the appliance for persistence and pivoting — distinguished from legitimate FortiGuard update / signature traffic by destination. Rationale: Article explicitly cites historical pattern: 'Fortinet security flaws are often exploited in ransomware attacks ... and in cyber espionage campaigns to breach the targets' networks.' Compromised FortiSandbox appliances are typical pivot points — they have outbound permission for FortiGuard updates, which attackers abuse to blend C2 traffic. Cross-checked: CISA KEV listing 13 Fortinet vulns abused by ransomware. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/critical-fortinet-fortisandbox-flaws-now-exploited-in-attacks/ • https://www.runzero.com/blog/fortinet-fortisandbox/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • FortiGuard signature/sandbox-engine updates (whitelist *.fortinet.com / *.fortiguard.com)
  • NTP synchronization to pool.ntp.org or corporate NTP
  • SNMP/Syslog forwarding to the SOC SIEM
  • Sandbox-detonation outbound — FortiSandbox detonating malware samples may legitimately reach malicious infrastructure as part of dynamic analysis (this is by design, scope to the management interface IP rather than the detonation NIC)
Suppression filter
| where not(DestinationHostName has_any ("fortinet", "fortiguard", "forticloud"))
| where DestinationPort !in (123, 514)  // exclude NTP and syslog
| where DestinationIP !in (CorporateInfraIPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is the FortiSandbox MANAGEMENT interface (not the detonation NIC, which legitimately reaches the open internet). Look up destination IPs/domains in threat intel — VirusTotal, AbuseIPDB, ThreatFox. Sample destinations: are they short-lived dynamic DNS (duckdns, no-ip), unfamiliar VPS providers (Choopa, BL Networks), or known C2 infrastructure? 2) Contain: if confirmed unauthorized egress, isolate the FortiSandbox from the network (preserve volatile memory if forensics planned), and immediately verify patch level on remaining sandbox appliances. 3) Hunt: extract the FortiSandbox running-config, look for newly-added admin accounts, modified DNS settings, or scheduled tasks. Correlate the FortiSandbox source IP with prior UC1/UC2/UC3 hits to identify the initial entry point CVE.
let FortiSandboxIPs = dynamic(["10.0.0.0"]);  // <- replace with appliance inventory
let FortinetDomains = dynamic(["fortinet.com", "fortiguard.com", "fortinet.net", "forticloud.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where LocalIP in (FortiSandboxIPs)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not(RemoteUrl has_any (FortinetDomains))
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            BytesEstimate = countif(isnotempty(RemoteIP)) * 1500,
            DestIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 20),
            DestUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20),
            Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by LocalIP, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where ConnCount > 10 or array_length(DestIPs) > 5
| order by FirstSeen desc
let FortiSandboxIPs = dynamic(["10.0.0.0"]);  // <- replace with appliance inventory
let FortinetDomains = dynamic(["fortinet.com", "fortiguard.com", "fortinet.net", "forticloud.com", "fortiguard.net"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SourceIP in (FortiSandboxIPs)
| where DestinationIP !startswith "10." and DestinationIP !startswith "172.16." and DestinationIP !startswith "192.168."
| where not(DestinationHostName has_any (FortinetDomains))
     and not(DestinationDnsDomain has_any (FortinetDomains))
| summarize Conns = count(),
            BytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)),
            DestIPs = make_set(DestinationIP, 30),
            DestHosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 30),
            Ports = make_set(DestinationPort, 20),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
            by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where BytesOut > 1000000 or array_length(DestIPs) > 10 or array_length(Ports) > 5
| order by FirstSeen desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")

            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)

| order by files desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

Critical

Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-06-16 16 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Since late 2025, malware has been spreading rapidly through the Steam Workshop, the gaming platform's built-in service for players to create and share custom content. The attackers are primarily targeting gamers in China and Russia.

ATT&CKT1204.002 T1486 T1555.003

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Known IOC hash match — malicious Steam Workshop wallpaper payloads
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Wallpaper Engine spawning script interpreters or LOLBins · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Dozens of malicious wallpapers found on Steam Workshop: gamers’ accounts at risk
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] DarkKomet 'Synaptics.exe' masquerade dropped by Wallpaper Engine workshop content · [LLM] Steam Workshop wallpaper '._cache_GAME1.exe' launcher execution · [LLM] Trojanised AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-system path · [LLM] Persistence via Steam Workshop wallpaper content path in Run keys / Scheduled Tasks · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 callback to malicious wallpaper campaign infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Steam credential file (loginusers.vdf / ssfn*) accessed by non-Steam process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DarkKomet 'Synaptics.exe' masquerade dropped by Wallpaper Engine workshop content AIInstallation High
Hunts the article's named DarkKomet backdoor file 'Synaptics.exe' dropped or executed outside the legitimate Synaptics touchpad driver install path. The legitimate vendor binary lives under Program Files\Synaptics; any other location is suspicious and matches the Steam Workshop wallpaper drop chain described in the article. Rationale: Article body explicitly names 'Synaptics.exe (part of the DarkKomet malware family)' as the dropped backdoor. The Synaptics name is a known legitimate touchpad driver, so anchoring on the binary name outside the vendor path yields a high-fidelity, low-noise alert. IOC bundle of 13 MD5s lets the analyst confirm at the hash level on triage.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1204.002 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Synaptics driver installed via OEM image to a non-standard path (Lenovo/Dell reimaging)
  • Synaptics driver portable extracted to a tech bench for troubleshooting
  • Renamed dev binary named Synaptics.exe (extremely rare)
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull SHA256/MD5 of the binary and compare against the article's IOC list; check digital signature (legit Synaptics is signed by Synaptics Inc.). Inspect parent process — wallpaper32.exe / wallpaper64.exe / ._cache_GAME1.exe parents are convicting. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via Defender Live Response, kill the Synaptics.exe PID, quarantine the binary and any sibling files under the same drop folder. Step 3 — Hunt: search the rest of the fleet for the same MD5, for outbound connections to 120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29, and for Steam credential files (loginusers.vdf, ssfn*) accessed by non-Steam processes in the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName =~ "Synaptics.exe"
| where not(FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files (x86)\Synaptics\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\Synaptics.exe"
| where not(NewProcessName has @"\Program Files\Synaptics\" or NewProcessName has @"\Program Files (x86)\Synaptics\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Steam Workshop wallpaper '._cache_GAME1.exe' launcher execution AIInstallation High
Hunts the distinctively named secondary launcher '._cache_GAME1.exe' described in the article — it boots the decoy NTRaholic game while simultaneously installing the trojanised AggregatorHost.dll. The '._cache_' filename prefix is unusual for legitimate Windows software and is highly specific to this wallpaper campaign. Rationale: Article verbatim: 'an executable named ._cache_GAME1.exe fires up to boot the actual game, NTRaholic' and 'that ._cache_GAME1.exe module is doing double duty. It simultaneously installs a custom version of a system library called AggregatorHost.dll'. The '._cache_' prefix is article-specific and extremely unusual in benign software.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Unity / Unreal asset cache files mis-extracted by user with .exe rename (rare)
  • Custom internal build pipeline staging artefacts with '._cache_' prefix
  • Mac-to-Windows file copy preserving Apple resource-fork '._' prefix on an exe (rare)
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the file's SHA256/MD5 and check against the article IOC list (13 MD5s). Identify the launching wallpaper package — usually under %ProgramFiles(x86)%\Steam\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\<id>\. Step 2 — Contain: kill the process tree (._cache_GAME1.exe, Synaptics.exe, any spawned child), isolate host, quarantine the wallpaper folder. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the Steam workshop content ID and check Steam Workshop subscription history; sweep the fleet for the same wallpaper subscription; check DeviceImageLoadEvents for AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-System32 paths.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName startswith "._cache_" and FileName endswith ".exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName matches regex @"(?i)\\\._cache_[^\\]+\.exe$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Wallpaper Engine spawning script interpreters or LOLBins AIExploitation High
Hunts for Wallpaper Engine (wallpaper32.exe / wallpaper64.exe / wallpaper_engine.exe) acting as the parent for cmd.exe, PowerShell, rundll32, regsvr32, mshta, or for unsigned binaries launched from %TEMP%/%APPDATA% — the execution mechanism the article describes as 'foreign code running directly on your computer' via application wallpapers. Rationale: Article body: 'application wallpapers ... essentially allows foreign code to be run directly on your computer ... Cybercriminals took note of this feature and started embedding malware right into these types of wallpapers.' The wallpaper32/64.exe → LOLBin or temp-folder-binary chain is the exact execution model. Steam Workshop content path 431960 is the official Wallpaper Engine Workshop ID.
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate 'application wallpaper' that embeds a third-party system monitor (e.g. CoreTemp, MSI Afterburner) — typically signed binaries from Program Files
  • Wallpaper Engine auto-updater launching a CEF helper from %APPDATA%
  • Twitch / Discord overlay started by an application wallpaper
  • Game wallpaper that legitimately calls cmd.exe to query system info
Suppression filter
and not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/c wmic","systeminfo") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "SystemMonitor")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the child SHA256 and check signature; pull the parent's command line which contains the workshop content ID (path '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\<id>\'). Cross-check that ID against active Steam Workshop reports. Step 2 — Contain: kill the child process tree, quarantine the workshop content folder, unsubscribe the user from the malicious wallpaper via Steam client (or block file write/read on the folder if Steam is critical). Step 3 — Hunt: for every host where this fired, search DeviceFileEvents for files written under the workshop content folder, and DeviceNetworkEvents for connections initiated by wallpaper32/64.exe or its children to 120.48.156.17 / 202.144.192.29.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","wallpaper_engine.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or FolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("wallpaper32.exe","wallpaper64.exe","wallpaper_engine.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
   or NewProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanised AggregatorHost.dll loaded from non-system path AIInstallation High
Hunts for AggregatorHost.dll loaded from any folder other than %SystemRoot%\System32 / SysWOW64. The article states the malicious '._cache_GAME1.exe' installs a custom AggregatorHost.dll that hijacks the user's Steam session — the legitimate DLL ships only inside the Windows install. Rationale: Article: 'a custom version of a system library called AggregatorHost.dll with a payload inside. This modified library has one main objective: track down the Steam app on the computer and hunt for account credentials.' Legitimate AggregatorHost ships only under %SystemRoot%, so any drop / load from elsewhere is highly fishy and article-specific.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005 T1056.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Microsoft KIR / SFC repair operation staging the DLL in %TEMP% during a Windows component refresh (rare)
  • IT-deployed sysprep capture extracting Windows components to a build directory
  • Developer testing a custom WAM authentication broker outside System32
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("trustedinstaller.exe","tiworker.exe","sfc.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: hash-verify the loaded DLL against the Microsoft signed binary catalog (signtool / get-authenticodesignature). Confirm parent process — _cache_GAME1.exe or other wallpaper-launched binaries are convicting. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, dump and quarantine the rogue DLL plus any Synaptics.exe sibling, kill the loading process. Force Steam logout for the affected user and rotate the Steam password + revoke active sessions. Step 3 — Hunt: search the fleet for additional AggregatorHost.dll loads from non-system paths over 30d; correlate with DeviceNetworkEvents to 120.48.156.17/ey.php which is the exfil endpoint the rogue DLL uses.
union
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
   | where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
   | where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\" or FolderPath has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\" or FolderPath has @"\Windows\WinSxS\")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventKind = "ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
   | where FileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"
   | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
   | where not(FolderPath has @"\Windows\System32\" or FolderPath has @"\Windows\SysWOW64\" or FolderPath has @"\Windows\WinSxS\")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventKind = strcat("File:",ActionType), FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, MD5, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFileName =~ "AggregatorHost.dll"

| NOT TargetFileName=/\\Windows\\(System32|SysWOW64|WinSxS)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count())

Steam credential file (loginusers.vdf / ssfn*) accessed by non-Steam process AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for non-Steam processes opening the Steam login persistence files (loginusers.vdf, config.vdf, ssfn*) — the AggregatorHost.dll trojan described in the article reads these to hijack the live Steam session. Anything but steam.exe / steamwebhelper.exe / steamservice.exe touching them is a high-fidelity infostealer signal. Rationale: Article: 'the modified library hijacks the user's live Steam session ... sends all the collected data to a server controlled by the hackers at hxxp://120.48.156[.]17/ey.php'. Steam session hijack requires reading loginusers.vdf / ssfn token files. Excluding the canonical Steam executables yields almost-zero baseline noise.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Steam Cloud backup utility from Valve
  • Steam family sharing config sync tool
  • User-installed Steam library manager (e.g. SLM)
  • AV scanner with non-standard process name reading the file on access
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !has "Valve"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the reading process and its SHA256, compare against the article's IOC list. Pivot the process tree to find the parent — wallpaper32/64.exe or ._cache_GAME1.exe are convicting. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, kill the offending process, force Steam logout via Steam Support (revokes ssfn tokens), reset Steam password, enable Steam Guard. Step 3 — Hunt: across the fleet, look for additional reads of \Steam\config\* by non-Steam parents; pivot on the reading binary's hash to find every host that ran it; sweep DeviceNetworkEvents for callbacks to 120.48.156.17/ey.php.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FolderPath has @"\Steam\config\" and (FileName in~ ("loginusers.vdf","config.vdf") or FileName startswith "ssfn"))
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe","steamerrorreporter64.exe","steam_bootstrap.exe","explorer.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Steam\config\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("loginusers.vdf","config.vdf") or TargetFileName startswith "ssfn"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("steam.exe","steamservice.exe","steamwebhelper.exe","steamerrorreporter.exe","steamerrorreporter64.exe","steam_bootstrap.exe","explorer.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 callback to malicious wallpaper campaign infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections from any process to the article's named C2 IPs (120.48.156.17, 202.144.192.29) or to the article's named C2 URL paths (/ey.php, /audit.php, /download2/Themes2.zip). These IOCs are confirmed by Kaspersky's IoC bundle. Rationale: Article verbatim names hxxp://120.48.156[.]17/ey.php as the Steam-session exfil endpoint and the IoC bundle cites http://202.144.192[.]29/audit.php and /download2/Themes2.zip as additional C2/payload URLs. IP-pinned hosting (not a CDN) keeps FPs at near zero.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • In-house malware sandbox detonating a sample with internet access
  • Threat-intel team manually browsing the C2 from a research VM
  • Security vendor downloading the sample via proxy with the analyst's user-agent
Suppression filter
and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("detonator.exe","sandbox.exe","cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the initiating process (InitiatingProcessFileName + SHA256). If the SHA matches the IOC list, treat as confirmed compromise. Otherwise spot-check process tree for wallpaper32/64.exe / ._cache_*.exe / Synaptics.exe ancestors. Step 2 — Contain: block 120.48.156.17 and 202.144.192.29 at egress / perimeter / Defender Network Protection; isolate host; force Steam credential rotation and revoke active sessions for the user. Step 3 — Hunt: 30-day sweep of DNS + netflow for the same IPs; pivot the initiating SHA256 to find every host that ran the same loader; check DeviceFileEvents for AggregatorHost.dll drops on those hosts.
union
  (DeviceNetworkEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where RemoteIP in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
      or RemoteUrl has_any ("/ey.php","/audit.php","/download2/Themes2.zip")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","ConnectionSuccess")
   | where RemoteIP in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
      or RemoteUrl has_any ("/ey.php","/audit.php","/download2/Themes2.zip")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort=tostring(RemotePort), RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256=InitiatingProcessSHA256, InitiatingProcessAccountName)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DestinationIP in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
      or RequestURL has_any ("/ey.php","/audit.php","/download2/Themes2.zip")
   | project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceUserName),
  (ImNetworkSession
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where DstIpAddr in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29") or Url has_any ("/ey.php","/audit.php","/download2/Themes2.zip")
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkApplicationProtocol),
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where Name in ("120.48.156.17","202.144.192.29")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known IOC hash match — malicious Steam Workshop wallpaper payloads AIWeaponization High
Direct-match sweep for the 13 MD5s published in Kaspersky's IoC bundle across process creation, file write, and image load telemetry. Use as a one-shot retrohunt and as a low-noise ongoing alert. Rationale: Article publishes 13 MD5s in the IoC section — a direct hash sweep is the cheapest, highest-fidelity backstop to behavioural detections. Hash match alone is convicting; correlate with the C2/file/registry detections for full kill-chain context.
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • VirusTotal / Hybrid Analysis researcher manually executing one of the samples on a lab machine
  • AV vendor reverse engineering team sharing samples through the corporate file share
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm hash on disk, capture the binary, identify drop source (Steam Workshop content folder is the convicting parent path). Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, block all 13 MD5s in Defender ASR file-block / file-quarantine policy, push the hash list to firewall sandbox/proxy AV. Step 3 — Hunt: retrohunt 90 days for the same hashes; pivot on each host's Steam Workshop subscription list for the malicious wallpaper content ID; cross-reference with the C2 IP detection results.

union

  (DeviceFileEvents    | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where MD5 in (IOCs) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="DeviceFileEvents", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where MD5 in (IOCs) | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source="DeviceImageLoadEvents", FileName, FolderPath, MD5, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| order by Timestamp desc

Persistence via Steam Workshop wallpaper content path in Run keys / Scheduled Tasks AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for autorun keys (HKCU/HKLM Run, RunOnce, Image File Execution Options, scheduled tasks) whose target executable lives under the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop content folder (Steam app 431960) or whose target is the article's named binaries (Synaptics.exe, AggregatorHost.dll, ._cache_*.exe). Legitimate wallpapers do not need autorun keys outside of Wallpaper Engine itself. Rationale: Article: 'leave the victim's system infected with backdoors or crypto miners' — backdoors / miners need to survive reboot. Persistence pointing at the Steam Workshop content folder for app 431960 (Wallpaper Engine's Workshop ID) is article-specific. Also catches Run-key persistence pointing at the article's named binaries.
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005 T1574.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wallpaper Engine's own auto-start key (points at Program Files\Wallpaper Engine\, not workshop content — already filtered by the value-data match)
  • User installing a legitimate Workshop wallpaper that ships its own helper EXE and pins a Run key (unusual but possible)
  • Antivirus quarantine restore creating Run key pointing at restored Synaptics.exe in a non-vendor path
Suppression filter
and not (RegistryValueData has @"\Program Files (x86)\Steam\steamapps\common\wallpaper_engine\" and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "wallpaper64.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the offending Run/Scheduled-Task value; confirm the target binary's SHA256 against the IOC list. Identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — wallpaper32/64.exe or ._cache_*.exe are convicting. Step 2 — Contain: delete the Run key / scheduled task, kill any running instance of the target binary, quarantine the target file, isolate the host. Step 3 — Hunt: across fleet, look for any other Run/RunOnce/IFEO/SchedTask pointing at \steamapps\workshop\content\431960\; sweep DeviceFileEvents for the SHA256 of the persisted binary; verify whether the user has Steam Workshop subscriptions to identified malicious content IDs.
union
  (DeviceRegistryEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
   | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\", @"\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run")
   | where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\", "Synaptics.exe", "AggregatorHost.dll", "._cache_")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath),
  (DeviceEvents
   | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
   | where ActionType in ("ScheduledTaskCreated","ScheduledTaskUpdated")
   | where AdditionalFields has_any (@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\", "Synaptics.exe", "AggregatorHost.dll", "._cache_")
   | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, AdditionalFields)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImRegistryEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Image File Execution Options\")
   | where RegistryValueData has_any (@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\", "Synaptics.exe", "AggregatorHost.dll", "._cache_")
   | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
  (SecurityEvent
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
   | where EventID in (4698,4702)
   | where EventData has_any (@"\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\", "Synaptics.exe", "AggregatorHost.dll", "._cache_")
   | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, EventID, Activity, EventData)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Persistence Pointing at Wallpaper Engine Workshop Content or Campaign Binaries
id: 5d2f8c14-3b9a-4e02-9d61-6e3a7b1c4d09
description: Detects Registry Run/RunOnce/IFEO values or scheduled tasks whose target points into the Wallpaper Engine Steam Workshop content folder (Steam app 431960) or to the named campaign binaries (Synaptics.exe, AggregatorHost.dll, ._cache_*.exe).
references:
  - https://securelist.com/dozens-of-malicious-wallpapers-found-on-steam-workshop/120186/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/16
tags:
  - attack.t1547.001
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: registry_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_key:
    TargetObject|contains:
      - '\CurrentVersion\Run'
      - '\CurrentVersion\RunOnce'
      - '\Image File Execution Options\'
  selection_value:
    Details|contains:
      - '\steamapps\workshop\content\431960\'
      - 'Synaptics.exe'
      - 'AggregatorHost.dll'
      - '._cache_'
  condition: selection_key and selection_value
falsepositives:
  - Wallpaper Engine itself writing its own startup key — typically points at \Wallpaper Engine\wallpaper64.exe in Program Files, not the workshop content folder
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 (@TargetObject:(*\\CurrentVersion\\Run\\* OR *\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce\\* OR *\\Image?File?Execution?Options\\* OR *\\currentversion\\run\\*)) (@Details:(*\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\* OR *Synaptics.exe* OR *synaptics.exe* OR *AggregatorHost.dll* OR *aggregatorhost.dll* OR *._cache_*))
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate (RegObjectName=/\\CurrentVersion\\(Run|RunOnce)/i OR RegObjectName=/\\Image File Execution Options\\/i) (RegStringValue=/\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\/i OR RegStringValue=/Synaptics\.exe/i OR RegStringValue=/AggregatorHost\.dll/i OR RegStringValue=/\._cache_/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Registry WHERE (Registry.registry_path LIKE "%\\CurrentVersion\\Run%" OR Registry.registry_path LIKE "%\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce%" OR Registry.registry_path LIKE "%\\Image File Execution Options\\%") AND (Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\%" OR Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%Synaptics.exe%" OR Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%AggregatorHost.dll%" OR Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%._cache_%.exe%") BY Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Endpoint.Registry WHERE (Registry.registry_path LIKE "%\\CurrentVersion\\Run%" OR Registry.registry_path LIKE "%\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce%" OR Registry.registry_path LIKE "%\\Image File Execution Options\\%") AND (Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%\\steamapps\\workshop\\content\\431960\\%" OR Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%Synaptics.exe%" OR Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%AggregatorHost.dll%" OR Registry.registry_value_data LIKE "%._cache_%.exe%") BY Registry.dest Registry.user Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.registry_value_data Registry.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("202.144.192.29", "120.48.156.17") or RemoteUrl has_any ("brightly.to")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["202.144.192.29", "120.48.156.17"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["brightly.to"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |

    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a

references:

    selection_domain:

            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'

falsepositives:

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("brightly.to")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.

    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")

| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)

| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer). → [LLM] Hosts vulnerable to CVE-2023-24932 with internet exposure (SprySOCKS UEFI bootkit pre-position)
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Windows version of SprySOCKS Linux malware used to attack govt orgs
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SprySOCKS DriverLoader (fsdiskbit.sys) write / image load on Windows endpoint · [LLM] SprySOCKS WIN_DRV IFEO persistence on vds.exe · [LLM] SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS persistence as Windows Print Processor (VSPMsg) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SprySOCKS DriverLoader (fsdiskbit.sys) write / image load on Windows endpoint AIInstallation High
Hunts for the WIN_DRV stage-zero driver 'fsdiskbit.sys' (DriverLoader) being dropped to disk or loaded as an image. fsdiskbit.sys is signed with a leaked certificate from the GitHub PastDSE project and is the loader that maps the in-memory RawWNPF rootkit driver. The filename is article-specific and not associated with any benign vendor. Rationale: fsdiskbit.sys and the DriverLoader designation are explicitly named in the ESET-sourced article body as the WIN_DRV first-stage. Filename has no overlap with legitimate Microsoft / vendor drivers per public driver databases. Earth Lusca/FishMonger attribution corroborated via ESET Operation FishMedley write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/operation-fishmedley/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/23/i/earth-lusca-employs-new-linux-backdoor.html
ATT&CKT1014 T1543.003 T1553.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • None expected with this exact filename — fsdiskbit.sys is not a known benign Windows driver
  • Forensic analyst extracting the IOC for sandboxing (use case context will explain)
  • Threat intel team copying the file to a malware library share
  • EDR live-response retrieval of the artifact for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull SHA256 of fsdiskbit.sys; check signer (PastDSE cert thumbprint) via DeviceFileCertificateInfo; confirm the file is signed by a non-MS cert and the writing process is not a known security tool. 2) Contain: Isolate host via MDE live response, block the SHA256 across the org, terminate any process loading the driver and capture a memory image for the RawWNPF in-memory driver. 3) Hunt: Pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet, look for IFEO\\vds.exe persistence (companion UC), VSPMsg print-processor registration, and outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket beacons from svchost / print spooler children.
let lookback = 14d;
let driverWrites = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "fsdiskbit.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventKind="FileWrite", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName;
let driverLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName =~ "fsdiskbit.sys"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, EventKind="ImageLoad", FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=tostring(""), InitiatingProcessAccountName;
driverWrites
| union driverLoads
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 14d;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where TargetFileName =~ "fsdiskbit.sys"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS WIN_DRV IFEO persistence on vds.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts for Image File Execution Options registry-key writes targeting vds.exe (Virtual Disk Service) — the IFEO-hijack persistence path used by SprySOCKS WIN_DRV to launch DriverLoader. ESET explicitly names vds.exe as the IFEO debugger target. Rationale: vds.exe IFEO is named verbatim in the article as the WIN_DRV persistence mechanism. IFEO writes targeting a specific binary like vds.exe are extremely rare in normal use — Application Verifier and AppCompat are the only common writers, neither targets vds.exe. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/operation-fishmedley/
ATT&CKT1546.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer enabling Application Verifier against vds.exe (extremely rare)
  • WinDbg gflags being set during driver debugging by a Microsoft support engineer
  • Endpoint hardening tool writing MitigationOptions to multiple system binaries (would hit other binaries too — pivot on whether vds.exe is the only target)
  • Manual VSS / disk troubleshooting where an admin attached a debugger
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("verifier.exe","gflags.exe","appverif.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/enable","-enable"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Inspect RegistryValueData — if it points to a non-Microsoft-signed binary in C:\\Windows\\System32 / C:\\ProgramData / user-writeable path, treat as confirmed. Pull SHA256 of the debugger image. 2) Contain: Delete the IFEO Debugger value, isolate the host, block the debugger SHA256. Note vds.exe runs as SYSTEM when storage operations occur, so privesc has already happened. 3) Hunt: Search the fleet for the same RegistryValueData path, look for companion fsdiskbit.sys writes and VSPMsg print-processor registrations.
let lookback = 30d;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"Image File Execution Options\vds.exe"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("Debugger","GlobalFlag","VerifierDlls","MitigationOptions","ReportingMode")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where RegistryKey has @"Image File Execution Options\vds.exe"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("Debugger","GlobalFlag","VerifierDlls","MitigationOptions")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS persistence as Windows Print Processor (VSPMsg) AIInstallation High
Hunts for registration of a Print Processor named VSPMsg under the Print Environments registry tree — the persistence mechanism used by SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS to load its DLL into spoolsv.exe at SYSTEM. The processor name VSPMsg is article-specific. Rationale: The processor name VSPMsg is explicitly called out in the article as the SprySOCKS WIN_PLUS persistence registration. Print Processor registrations are rare overall and the specific VSPMsg name carries no legitimate vendor association. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/operation-fishmedley/
ATT&CKT1547.012
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate printer driver vendor (HP/Canon/Brother) registering a new processor — name will not be VSPMsg
  • MSI-based printer driver install via msiexec.exe (filtered by InitiatingProcessFileName)
  • Sysadmin running prndrvr.exe to install drivers (filtered)
  • Windows Update servicing the spooler (rare, runs as TrustedInstaller)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","prndrvr.exe","setup.exe","trustedinstaller.exe") and not (RegistryValueData has "VSPMsg"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: Read RegistryValueData — the value will be the DLL filename of the Print Processor. Pull SHA256 and signer of that DLL from DeviceFileEvents / DeviceImageLoadEvents in C:\\Windows\\System32\\spool\\prtprocs\\. 2) Contain: Stop the Print Spooler service, remove the registry key and the dropped DLL, isolate the host. Spooler runs as SYSTEM so privesc has occurred. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the DLL hash org-wide, look for spoolsv.exe spawning unexpected children, outbound TCP/UDP/WebSocket beacons from spoolsv.exe, and companion fsdiskbit.sys / IFEO\\vds.exe persistence on the same host.
let lookback = 30d;
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\" and RegistryKey has @"\Print Processors\"
| where RegistryKey has "VSPMsg" or RegistryValueData has "VSPMsg" or RegistryValueName =~ "Driver"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("spoolsv.exe","msiexec.exe","setup.exe","prndrvr.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessIntegrityLevel
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Control\Print\Environments\" and RegistryKey has @"\Print Processors\"
| where RegistryKey has "VSPMsg" or RegistryValueData has "VSPMsg"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Hosts vulnerable to CVE-2023-24932 with internet exposure (SprySOCKS UEFI bootkit pre-position) AIWeaponization Medium
Posture hunt for endpoints still vulnerable to CVE-2023-24932 (BlackLotus / Secure Boot bypass), the flaw ESET telemetry suggests SprySOCKS may exploit as a UEFI bootkit component. Prioritises internet-facing devices that match the campaign's government-org targeting profile. Rationale: CVE-2023-24932 is explicitly named in the article as the Secure Boot flaw the suspected UEFI bootkit component might exploit. The vulnerability requires an active mitigation step (revocation) beyond the May 2023 patch; many fleets still carry vulnerable bootmgr versions. Cross-checked Microsoft MSRC advisory and Huntress threat library. Cross-checked against: • https://msrc.microsoft.com/update-guide/vulnerability/CVE-2023-24932 • https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/topic/how-to-manage-the-windows-boot-manager-revocations-for-secure-boot-changes-associated-with-cve-2023-24932-41a975df-beb2-40c1-99a3-b3ff139f832d • https://www.huntress.com/threat-library/vulnerabilities/cve-2023-24932
ATT&CKT1542.003 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Patched hosts where the May 2023 KB is installed but the Secure Boot revocation step (KB5025885 manual step) has not been applied — TVM correctly flags these as still-vulnerable
  • Servers where reboot has been deferred indefinitely
  • Air-gapped / standalone devices that haven't pulled the revocation update
  • Hosts whose UEFI firmware doesn't support the DBX revocation update yet
Response runbook
1) Triage: Filter the result set to internet-facing assets and government-org-priority workloads (foreign-affairs, telecom, defence). Confirm KB5025885 (or successor) status. 2) Contain: Apply the manual Secure Boot revocation steps per KB5025885 starting with internet-facing tier-0 assets; reboot in maintenance window. Enable HVCI + Memory Integrity where missing. 3) Hunt: On all CVE-2023-24932-vulnerable hosts, search DeviceFileEvents for fsdiskbit.sys writes, DeviceRegistryEvents for IFEO\\vds.exe and Print\\Environments\\VSPMsg entries, and DeviceEvents for ActionType 'DeviceBootIntegrityChanged' or unexpected EFI partition writes.

C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
